snippet.title: The ENTIRE History of Mali Empire | King Crashed Global Economy by Going on Holiday | Documentary
snippet.description:
At its height, the Mali Empire was one of the largest, richest, and most influential civilizations on Earth. While much of medieval Europe struggled through war, famine, and plague, Mali controlled vast trade networks, governed legendary cities like Timbuktu, and helped shape the global flow of gold.

This documentary explores the entire history of the Mali Empire, from the rise of the Mandinka in West Africa and the fall of the Ghana Empire, to the legendary story of Sundiata Keita, the creation of Mali, and the reign of Mansa Musa, the richest ruler in recorded history. We follow the empire through its golden age of trade, scholarship, and Islamic culture, and into the long centuries of political decline, invasion, and historical erasure.

You’ll discover how Mali became the economic heart of the medieval world, why Timbuktu became one of history’s great centers of learning, and how the memory of this empire survived through oral tradition, manuscripts, and the enduring legacy of West Africa itself.

From gold and salt trade routes to Mansa Musa’s world-shaking pilgrimage, this is the story of one of history’s greatest empires — and why it still matters today.

If you enjoy long-form history documentaries on forgotten empires, lost civilizations, and the forces that shaped the world, subscribe for more.

snippet.title: Exploring The Forbidden Ruins Of Hitler’s Eastern Headquarters
snippet.description:
Deep in the forests of modern-day Poland lie the shattered remains of the Wolf’s Lair, the most important Nazi command center of WW2. In this documentary, we explore the 800 days Adolf Hitler spent within these concrete walls, making the catastrophic decisions that led to the fall of the Soviet Union and eventually his own Reich. From secret drug injections to the daring assassination attempt by Klouse von Stalenberg, we uncover the true story of Hitler’s isolation, his growing paranoia, and the hubris that built the largest bunker complex in history.

snippet.title: Derinkuyu: The Underground City — Who Built It, Why They Hid & What They Feared
snippet.description:
In the Cappadocia region of Turkey lies Derinkuyu — an underground city carved from volcanic rock that housed an estimated 20,000 people across eighteen stories descending 85 meters beneath the earth. Discovered by accident in 1963 when a resident broke through his basement wall, this ancient refuge represents one of the most sophisticated examples of survival architecture ever created by human hands.

But who built Derinkuyu? When? And most pressingly: what threat was terrible enough that entire populations chose to live in darkness, sealed behind massive rolling stone doors, rather than face whatever horror awaited on the surface?

This documentary explores the complete documented history of Derinkuyu — from its likely origins during the Hittite or Phrygian period (1200-700 BC) through its extensive use by Byzantine Christians fleeing Arab-Byzantine warfare, to its abandonment in the medieval period and rediscovery in the modern age.

snippet.title: When the War Ended… She Refused to Go Back Home | History for Sleep
snippet.description:
When wars come to an end, history often focuses on treaties, victories, and the return of soldiers, yet for many individuals the transition back to ordinary life was far more complicated. In this calm, sleep-friendly history episode, we explore the story behind a woman who, after years shaped by conflict, uncertainty, and profound change, chose not to return to the life she once knew. Through the broader experiences of women living during and after times of war, we examine how conflict could transform identities, relationships, opportunities, and expectations in ways that continued long after the fighting had ceased. For some, wartime responsibilities brought new forms of independence, employment, education, and social freedom that had been difficult to imagine before. Returning home sometimes meant returning to old limitations, familiar routines, or communities that no longer felt the same. Across different periods of history, women found themselves navigating difficult choices between duty, family expectations, personal ambitions, and the realities of a world that had been permanently changed by war. Their stories reveal not only the hardships of conflict but also the resilience, adaptability, and quiet courage required to build a new future when peace finally arrived. Daily life after war often involved rebuilding homes, restoring communities, reconnecting with loved ones, and deciding what parts of the past should be carried forward into the future. While every story was unique, many shared a common theme: the realization that neither people nor places remained exactly as they had been before. As evening settles over quiet streets and distant memories fade into history, this gentle retelling invites you to relax and drift toward sleep while exploring the human choices that sometimes followed the end of war.

snippet.title: The Tinderbox: Understanding The Israeli-Palestinian Conflict
snippet.description:
THE TINDERBOX: understanding Israel/Palestine
We will never find peace unless we address the basic problem.

A rare and thought-provoking examination of both sides of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, from its catalyst to why it still rages, to what needs to happen for it to stop.

The Tinderbox combines ancient and more recent history, geopolitical problems (racism, inequality, immigration and fake truths), and psychology, with the deeply personal journey of one person forced to challenge everything they’d been taught about the conflict in Israel and Palestine.

The film also shows the human face of this conflict by hearing from a wide variety of contemporary voices, ranging from a Settler to a political member of Hamas. Today, while this conflict still rages, an American Middle East Peace Plan is in the works, and anti-Semitism and Islamophobia remain as globally controversial as ever, this film will provide context, show how history continues to play out in the daily lives of people on either side of the divide, and will empower audiences to make up their own minds.

snippet.title: The Dark Folklore They Tried to Erase: What Fairies Really Were | Complete Documentary
snippet.description:
Close your eyes and picture a fairy. Do you see Tinkerbell? A fairy godmother? Tiny wings and sparkles?

That's not what fairies were.

This is the complete, unfiltered history of what fairies actually were in authentic folklore—before Disney, before Victorian sanitization, before we made them safe for children.

The real fairies stole children from their cradles. They hunted humans for sport. They demanded blood tribute. They were gods in exile, spirits of the land, beings so dangerous that entire villages lived in terror of offending them.

Tonight, we journey into the forgotten darkness of British and Celtic fairy folklore. We'll explore:

- The Seelie and Unseelie Courts: Light and Dark kingdoms locked in eternal war
- Changelings: The horrifying truth about stolen children
- The Redcap: A murderer who soaked his cap in human blood
- Banshees and Kelpies: Death omens and water predators
- Puck and household spirits: The fairies who lived alongside humans
- The Victorian Sanitization: How we erased the truth
- What we lost when we made fairies harmless

This isn't children's entertainment. This is survival knowledge encoded in story. This is what our ancestors knew in their bones: that the world is stranger and more dangerous than we remember.

I am Mr. Ravenhurst. And this is the dark truth about fairies.

Percocet was created to help people manage pain. Instead, it became one of the defining drugs of a generation—and one of the deadliest. Throughout the 2010s and early 2020s, opioid addiction spread through communities across America, leaving a devastating impact on millions of families. The music industry was not spared. Some of hip-hop's most talented artists openly referenced Percocet and other opioids in their lyrics, while many struggled with addiction behind the scenes.

In this video, we explore how Percocet became intertwined with modern rap culture and the broader opioid crisis. Discover the history of oxycodone, why Percocet became so widely prescribed, and how prescription opioid misuse evolved into a public health disaster. Learn about the lives and careers of artists including Juice WRLD, Mac Miller, Big Scarr, and others whose struggles reflected a larger epidemic affecting an entire generation.

snippet.title: Crash Course Scientific Thinking Preview
snippet.description:
Science is one of the best ways we have of understanding what’s going on around us. In Crash Course Scientific Thinking we’ll explore the foundational principles that underlie scientific thought. 

Course Description
In 7 episodes, Crash Course Scientific Thinking will teach learners the foundational principles underlying scientific thought, pulling back the curtain on processes like peer review, interrogating what makes sources reliable (or not), unpacking how consensus is reached, and revealing how scientific understanding changes over time. Ultimately, learners will gain the ability to think more critically about the scientific information they encounter in their everyday lives. 

Series Objectives
- Describe the dynamic, communal nature of science, articulating the roles of uncertainty and consensus.
- Explain the role of peer review and replication in science.
- Unpack the potential for bias and error in science and understand its self-correction mechanisms.
- Understand the role of specialization in scientific expertise.
- Interpret primary, secondary, and tertiary sources, and use lateral reading to verify claims.
- Understand basic statistical language used to describe scientific findings.

snippet.title: Ancient Nightmare Entities: From Lilith to the Medieval Mare — 5,000 Years of Sleep Demons
snippet.description:
For five thousand years, humans have documented the same terrifying experience: waking in darkness, unable to move, sensing a malevolent presence in the room. The ancient Sumerians called her Lilith. The Greeks called it ephialtes. Medieval Europeans knew her as the mare—the night-hag that gave nightmares their very name.

This is the complete scholarly history of nightmare entities across human civilization—from Mesopotamian demons to Victorian occultism. We examine why every culture, despite having no contact with each other, described identical experiences. Why protective rituals from iron to prayer showed correlation with reduced episodes. And what these ancient encounters reveal about the universal human experience of sleep paralysis.

snippet.description:
Hey guys! We’re now live on Spotify 🎧

The strongest drugs in a hospital are not always the ones patients fear most. Some are lifesaving, some are routine, and some can quietly lead to dependence when pain, anxiety, surgery, and recovery collide.

In this video, we rank common hospital medications by how likely they are to become addictive, from powerful opioids like fentanyl, morphine, Dilaudid, and oxycodone to benzodiazepines, stimulants, sleep medications, and lower-risk drugs used for pain, nausea, and sedation. This is not medical advice, but a clear look at why certain prescriptions carry a higher risk of misuse, tolerance, withdrawal, and addiction.

snippet.title: Crash Course Geology Preview

Welcome to Crash Course Geology! Over the course of 25 episodes, Sage will introduce you to the incredible geological forces, cycles, and processes that shape our world. This series will explore how geology touches all of our lives — and connects us to a much bigger story.

Course Description
In 25 episodes, we’re going to learn about geology—the study of Earth’s physical structure and processes. Our host, Sage, will teach you about the geological forces and cycles that shape our planet’s past, present, and future. 

This content is based on an introductory university-level curriculum. By the end of this course, you should be able to: 

Trace Earth’s development from its earliest periods to its current structure
Understand the forces of plate tectonics and how they shape Earth’s landscape
Describe the formation of geologic elements like minerals, rocks, and gems 
Identify geologic forces and cycles that impact the earth, while dispelling myths about extreme geological hazards
Learn what geology reveals about Earth’s distant past and what it can teach us about our current changing climate
Explore the geology of other planets within the context of Earth’s unique and common qualities and phenomena
Become familiar with different specialities within geology and what different types of geologists do

Key texts cited include:
Marshak, Stephen. 2021. Earth: Portrait of a Planet, Seventh Edition.
Babcock, Loren E. 2009. Gemstones and Precious Metals.

snippet.title: Madame Guillotine and Revolutionary France | History for Sleep
snippet.description:
In the closing years of the eighteenth century, France experienced one of the most dramatic transformations in modern history. Ancient traditions gave way to sweeping political change, familiar institutions disappeared, and ordinary people found themselves living through an age of uncertainty unlike anything their ancestors had known. In this calm, sleep-friendly history episode, we explore the story of Revolutionary France through the symbol that came to define the era—"Madame Guillotine."

Originally introduced as a more standardized and supposedly humane method of capital punishment, the guillotine quickly became one of the most recognizable symbols of the French Revolution. Yet behind its powerful image was a far broader story of changing governments, crowded Parisian streets, shifting loyalties, economic hardship, public ceremonies, newspapers, marketplaces, and the everyday lives of millions of ordinary French citizens navigating an uncertain future.

This gentle historical journey explores pre-revolutionary society, the fall of the monarchy, life in revolutionary Paris, the National Convention, changing political factions, the Reign of Terror, revolutionary festivals, daily life, food shortages, fashion, public opinion, and the gradual emergence of a new France. Through letters, newspapers, memoirs, court records, and contemporary accounts, we discover how one nation experienced profound political and social change while ordinary families continued to work, eat, raise children, and hope for stability.

The video also reflects on the atmosphere of Revolutionary France — narrow cobbled streets filled with conversation, church bells echoing across Paris, busy market squares, handwritten pamphlets changing hands, candlelight illuminating modest homes, and citizens quietly wondering what tomorrow might bring.

As evening settles over the city and the sounds of the day slowly fade into silence, this peaceful retelling invites you to relax and drift toward sleep while discovering the remarkable history of Madame Guillotine and Revolutionary France.

snippet.title: How Spain Accidentally Conquered the Philippines | 333 Years of Empire
snippet.description:
Spain never set out to colonize the Philippines. It was hunting for spices and a shortcut to the Moluccas. Instead it stumbled into 333 years of rule over 7,000 islands, a conquest that would make the Philippines the largest Catholic nation in Asia and reshape Southeast Asia forever.

This is the complete story, from the barangays and sultanates that thrived before Magellan's fateful arrival in 1521, through Legazpi's conquest, the galleon trade that linked Asia and the Americas, the brutal encomienda system, centuries of revolts and Moro resistance, the rise of Rizal and the Katipunan, and the revolution that finally ended Spanish rule, only for the islands to be sold to the United States in 1898.

snippet.title: The ENTIRE History of the AZTEC EMPIRE | How Refugees Conquered the Americas | Documentary
snippet.description:
What if the most powerful empire in the Americas was built by people nobody wanted?

The Aztecs didn't begin as conquerors. They began as refugees — wandering outcasts begging for scraps of swamp and rock in a valley where everyone else had already claimed their place. Within two centuries, they built Tenochtitlan, a city of 200,000 people at a time when London had fewer than 60,000. A gleaming island metropolis of aqueducts, floating gardens, and pyramids that stunned even the hardened Spanish soldiers who first laid eyes on it.

Then, in 75 days, it was gone.

In this documentary, we trace the full extraordinary story of the Mexica — from their mythic origins in Aztlan, through decades of humiliation and vassalage, to the Triple Alliance that shattered Tepanec power and launched one of history's most astonishing empires. We'll explore the engineering genius of Tenochtitlan, the brutal logic of Aztec sacrifice, the philosopher king Nezahualcoyotl, and the invisible conqueror that did more damage than any Spanish sword.

This is not the story of savages defeated by civilization. This is the story of one of humanity's greatest achievements — and how it was buried, deliberately, beneath the city you know as Mexico City.

snippet.title: The ENTIRE History of CUBA | 500 Years of Revolution, Resistance, and Survival | History Documentary
snippet.description:
Why does a tiny island of eleven million people keep the entire world on edge?

Spain bled for it for nearly four hundred years. The United States invaded it twice, blockaded it, funded an army to take it back, and plotted to assassinate its leader more than six hundred times. The Soviet Union nearly started a nuclear war over it. Cuba has no oil, no nuclear arsenal, no great military power. And yet every empire of the modern era has been willing to risk everything to control it — or destroy it.

Tonight, we tell the complete story. All of it. Five hundred years of conquest, slavery, revolution, Cold War brinkmanship, and sixty years of defiance that still isn't finished.

We begin before Columbus — with the Taíno people who built a thriving civilization across this island for over a thousand years, only to be erased within a single generation of European contact. Then comes the Spanish conquest, the turning of Havana into the nerve center of an entire Atlantic empire, the sugar boom that swallowed the island whole, and the hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans whose labor built every ounce of that wealth.

Then the wars. The Ten Years' War, which burned the eastern provinces and produced heroes that Cuba still carries in its bones. José Martí, the poet-revolutionary who saw the American threat coming decades before anyone else and died on horseback before he could stop it. The War of Independence, won in the mountains and then stolen at the surrender ceremony where no Cuban was invited. The Platt Amendment, which handed Cuba a constitution with a leash already attached.

Then the republic — the Dance of the Millions, the mob casinos, the Havana nightlife built on the misery of the countryside. Batista's coup, which took seventy-seven minutes and ended Cuban democracy without firing a single shot. The Moncada Barracks, where a young lawyer stood before a court that wanted to imprison him and told it calmly that history would absolve him instead.

And then the revolution. The Granma landing in a mangrove swamp. The Sierra Maestra. Che Guevara. The Bay of Pigs — one of the most complete humiliations in CIA history. Thirteen days in October nineteen sixty-two when the world held its breath and waited to see whether civilization would survive the week. The Special Period, when the Soviet Union collapsed and Cuba lost eighty-five percent of its trade overnight and somehow, impossibly, held on.

And finally, the uncertain present. Fidel's death. The protests of July two thousand twenty-one, the largest the island had seen in decades. A new generation with smartphones and no memory of the revolution, running out of patience with a system that runs out of food.

This is not the story of a small island. This is the story of what happens when geography, sugar, slavery, ideology, and the ambitions of great powers collide on the same patch of land — over and over again, for five centuries, without ever fully resolving.
Settle in. This one is worth it.

One moment you're talking to the doctor. The next, hours have passed—and you remember almost nothing. Versed, also known as midazolam, is one of the most commonly used hospital drugs in the world, famous for its ability to calm patients, induce sedation, and erase the memory of medical procedures in real time. But how does a drug make your memories simply disappear?

In this video, we explore the science and history of Versed (midazolam), from its development as a benzodiazepine to its widespread use before surgery, endoscopy, emergency procedures, and intensive care. Learn how it produces sedation and temporary amnesia, why hospitals rely on it, what patients typically experience, and the risks associated with respiratory depression, dependence, and misuse. We'll also explain why most people remember almost nothing after receiving this remarkable medication.

- How paid grief performers transitioned from funeral to pub
- Victorian funeral theater and commercial performance

- Elaborate glass-sided hearses with six black plumed horses
- Funeral costs bankrupting working families for years
- Death becoming comprehensive commercial service industry

- Resurrection men stealing fresh corpses for medical schools
- How grave robbers worked efficiently to extract bodies

- Competing funeral processions in Victorian neighborhoods

- Widows forced to wear black for 2+ years after husband's death
- Strict mourning rules controlling women's lives completely
- Queen Victoria's 40-year widowhood setting national standard
- Men wearing simple armband while women imprisoned in grief
- Social ostracism for breaking mourning etiquette

HAIR JEWELRY:
- Mourning jewelry crafted from deceased's actual hair
- Hair workers weaving intricate flowers from human hair strands
- Widows wearing multiple pieces containing dead family members
- Whitby jet industry employing hundreds for mourning jewelry

PROFESSIONAL MOURNERS:
- Mutes hired to walk in funeral processions looking sad

- How undertakers upsold grieving families at vulnerable moments

CHILD MORTALITY:
